cards.definition: Selling ownership (shares). Shareholders get the upside if the company does well but are paid last if it fails.
cards.example: A startup sells 20% of its shares to a venture fund for $10M.
cards.definitionMasked: Selling ownership (shares). Shareholders get the upside if the company does well but are paid last if it fails.
cards.exampleMasked: A startup sells 20% of its shares to a venture fund for $10M.

cards.definition: Borrowing money. Lenders get a fixed return and are paid before shareholders, but they don't share in the upside. Because lenders have no upside, they protect themselves with contract terms. Those terms are what deal-data platforms benchmark.
cards.example: A company borrows $300M, promising 6% a year and repayment in 2030; lenders get nothing extra if profits soar.

cards.definition: Both are debt securities sold to investors. "Notes" traditionally meant shorter maturities, but in practice the terms are used interchangeably. Most high-yield deals are called "Senior Notes."

cards.definition: One company buying or combining with another. Governed by a merger agreement (Section 8).
cards.example: Company A agrees to buy Company B for $4B in cash.

cards.definition: The question lawyers ask during negotiation: what is typical for comparable deals right now? Answering it requires extracting the same term from many contracts and comparing them.
cards.example: A lawyer asks: "Across 2025 high-yield deals, what share used a 101% change-of-control price?"
cards.why: This is the core of what deal-data platforms sell. A typical task is to compute a distribution (median, percentiles) of a term or flag deals that are "off market."

cards.definition: The amount borrowed and repaid at the end. Here, $500 million.
cards.why: Indentures also mention the minimum denomination (often $2,000 or $1,000). A parser that grabs that number instead of the deal size is a common bug.
cards.definitionMasked: The amount borrowed and repaid at the end. Here, $500 million.

cards.definition: 100% of face value. Prices are quoted as a percentage of par, so "redeem at 101%" means paying $1,010 per $1,000 bond.
cards.example: A bond quoted at a price of 100 trades at exactly its face value.

cards.definition: The annual interest, here 7.50%, usually paid in two semi-annual installments.

cards.definition: The contract governing a bond issue, between the issuer and a trustee. It sets out the payment terms, redemption rights, covenants and events of default. Often 100+ pages, organized into numbered articles and sections (e.g. "Section 4.10 Change of Control").
cards.example: A 140-page contract filed as Exhibit 4.1 that sets the notes' payment terms, covenants and defaults.
cards.why: This is the document you'd download and parse to extract bond terms. On EDGAR it is usually filed as Exhibit 4.x.

cards.definition: The company that borrows by selling the bonds.
cards.example: Acme Corp: the company that sells the notes and owes the interest.
cards.definitionMasked: The company that borrows by selling the bonds.
cards.exampleMasked: Acme Corp: the company that sells the notes and owes the interest.

cards.definition: A bank (e.g. U.S. Bank, Wilmington Trust, Computershare) that represents all bondholders. Thousands of investors can't negotiate individually, so the trustee enforces the indenture on their behalf.
cards.example: U.S. Bank, named in the bond contract to enforce it on behalf of all holders.

cards.definition: Where the debt ranks in the repayment line during bankruptcy. Senior debt is paid before subordinated (junior) debt.
cards.example: In bankruptcy, one class of noteholders is paid in full before a junior class receives anything.
cards.definitionMasked: Where the debt ranks in the repayment line during bankruptcy. _____ debt is paid before _____ (junior) debt.
cards.exampleMasked: In bankruptcy, one class of noteholders is paid in full before a junior class receives anything.

cards.definition: Secured debt is backed by collateral (specific assets lenders can seize), like a mortgage. Unsecured debt has no collateral. "Senior secured" is the safest position; "senior unsecured" is first in line among unsecured lenders.
cards.example: One tranche of lenders can seize the company's factories if it defaults; another tranche has no pledged assets.

cards.definition: Investment grade = rated BBB- or higher: safer, lower coupons, few covenants. High yield ("junk") = below BBB-: riskier, higher coupons, heavy covenants.
cards.example: A BBB- company pays 5% with few covenants; a B-rated company pays 9% with a 100-page covenant package.
cards.why: Most of the interesting "what's market" analysis is in high yield, where covenants are negotiated deal by deal.

cards.definition: The issuer's right to repay ("call") the bonds before maturity at a set price.
cards.example: Rates fall, so Acme repays its 7.5% notes early at 103.75% and refinances at 5%.

cards.definition: An initial window, often 2–3 years for high yield (described as "NC2" or "NC3"), when the bonds can't be called at normal prices.
cards.example: "NC3": for the first three years the notes can't be repaid early at normal prices.

cards.definition: After the non-call period, the call price starts above par and falls each year to par.
cards.example: Callable at 103.750% in year 3, 101.875% in year 4, and 100% thereafter. The first call premium is often half the coupon.
cards.definitionMasked: After the non-call period, the call price starts above par and falls each year to par.

cards.definition: During the non-call period, the issuer can still repay, but only by paying the present value of every remaining coupon (discounted at a Treasury rate plus a small spread, e.g. T+50bps). It's so expensive that it's effectively a penalty.
cards.example: In year 1, repaying the notes early costs the present value of every remaining coupon, discounted at Treasuries + 50bps.

cards.definition: An exception letting the issuer redeem a slice of the bonds early, usually up to 35–40%, using cash from a stock sale, at par plus one year's coupon.
cards.example: After its IPO, Acme uses the cash to redeem 35% of its 7.50% notes at 107.50%.

cards.definition: A defined event in which the company gets a new owner, e.g. an acquirer buys more than 50% of the voting stock, or the company sells substantially all its assets.
cards.example: A private equity firm buys 60% of Acme's voting stock.

cards.definition: Bondholders' right to force the company to buy back their bonds if a change of control occurs, almost always at **101%** of principal plus accrued interest. Protects lenders from a new owner who might load the company with more debt.
cards.example: Acme is acquired, and holders force it to buy back their notes at 101.
cards.why: 101% is so standard that any other value is "off market," which makes it a classic field to extract and benchmark.

cards.definition: Exemptions that let companies sell bonds without a full public registration. 144A covers sales to large US institutions ("qualified institutional buyers"); Reg S covers sales outside the US. Most high-yield bonds are sold this way.
cards.example: Notes sold only to large US institutions and to buyers outside the US, without a full SEC registration.
cards.why: Because 144A deals aren't registered, the indenture often appears on EDGAR only as an exhibit to an 8-K filed after closing.

cards.definition: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. A rough proxy for the cash a business generates from operations. Most covenant tests are built on it.
cards.example: Revenue of $1B minus $750M of operating costs = $250M, before interest, taxes and non-cash charges.

cards.definition: Total debt ÷ EBITDA. "4.0x levered" means debt equals four years of EBITDA. Higher = riskier.
cards.example: $1B of debt against $250M of EBITDA = 4.0x.

cards.definition: EBITDA ÷ interest expense. How many times over earnings cover interest payments. Lower = riskier. A typical test: coverage of at least 2.0x.
cards.example: $250M of EBITDA against $80M of interest expense = 3.1x.

cards.definition: A test the borrower must pass every quarter, like a quarterly checkup. Failing is a default even if the company did nothing new. Typical of bank loans.
cards.example: "Leverage must not exceed 4.5x at the end of any fiscal quarter."

cards.definition: A test checked only when the borrower tries to do something, such as borrow more or pay a dividend. Like a bouncer at a door: business can worsen and nothing triggers. Typical of bonds.
cards.example: Acme's leverage drifts up to 6x, but nothing is tested until it tries to borrow more or pay a dividend.

cards.definition: A size-capped exception to a covenant.

cards.definition: Core high-yield covenant restricting how much additional debt the company can take on, outside permitted baskets and ratio debt. More debt means a smaller share of the company for existing lenders.

cards.definition: Core high-yield covenant restricting pledging assets as collateral to other lenders, so other creditors can't jump ahead in line.

cards.definition: Core high-yield covenant restricting asset sales: sale proceeds must be reinvested in the business or used to repay debt within a set period.
